hook.line: Altamira's lawyer keeps raising his offer, and Tomás hasn't even looked at the number. When you want to say that nothing a person might do will change your mind, Spanish gives *aunque* a different verb form.
hook.es: Aunque Altamira me ofrezca más, no vendo el café.
hook.en: Even if Altamira offers me more, I'm not selling the café.

examples.en: Even if it rains, I'll go out.

examples.es: Aunque me ofrezcan un millón, no vendo.
examples.en: Even if they offer me a million, I'm not selling.

examples.es: Aunque Altamira pague bien, no nos vamos.
examples.en: Even if Altamira pays well, we're not leaving.
Even if it's expensive, I'll buy it.

examples.es: Aunque tengas razón, no voy a firmar.
examples.en: Even if you're right, I'm not going to sign.

examples.es: Por más que Altamira insista, no voy a firmar.
examples.en: However much Altamira insists, I'm not going to sign.
Are you going to go even if it rains?

rule:
Until now, *aunque* meant even though and took a plain verb, because you were stating a fact: *Aunque llueve, salgo.*

When the thing is only possible, or you don't care whether it's true, the verb changes ending: *Aunque llueva, saldré.* In English that is even if.

The switch is the vowel flip you already know from the subjunctive:
*-ar* verbs take *-e*: *llueva*, *pague*, *insista*.
*-er* and *-ir* verbs take *-a*: *tenga*, *haga*, *ofrezca* (it is *-ca* here).
Irregulars stay irregular: *sea*, *esté*, *vaya*, *sepa*.

*Por más que* and *por mucho que* work the same way and mean however much.

The main verb stays normal: *no vendo*, *saldré*, *no voy a firmar*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the concessive subjunctive: *aunque* with the subjunctive for a case that is possible or beside the point. In the next lesson you'll set it side by side with *aunque* plus the plain verb.

options: Even though it's raining, we go out.
Even if it rains, we go out.

readAndPick.es: Aunque Altamira pague bien, no vendemos.
options: Even if Altamira pays well, we're not selling.
Altamira pays well, so we're selling.
Even though Altamira pays well, we're not selling.
Even if it's late, we open.
Even though it was late, we opened.
Because it's late, we open.

readAndPick.es: Por más que Altamira insista, no voy a firmar.
options: Altamira insisted, so I'm going to sign.
However much Altamira insists, I'm not going to sign.
Because Altamira insists, I'm not going to sign.

readAndPick.es: Aunque tengas razón, no voy a firmar.
options: Even though you're right, I signed.
Because you're right, I'm not going to sign.
Even if you're right, I'm not going to sign.

readAndPick.es: Aunque me ofrezcan un millón, no vendo.
options: Even if they offer me a million, I'm not selling.
They offered me a million, but I'm not selling.
They offered me a million, so I'm selling.

readAndPick.es: Aunque no me guste, lo voy a hacer.
options: I don't like it, so I'm not going to do it.
Even if I don't like it, I'm going to do it.
I liked it, so I'm going to do it.

readAndPick.es: Aunque esté cansado, voy al trabajo.
options: Even if I'm tired, I'm going to work.
I'm not tired, so I'm going to work.
Because I'm tired, I'm not going to work.
Did you go even though it rained?
Are you going to go even if it rains?
Are you going because it rains?

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *llueve* or *llueva* and type the whole sentence: *Aunque ___, saldré.* (Even if it rains, I'll go out.)
yourTurn.why: Rain is only possible, not a fact yet, so the verb takes the *-a* ending of *llover*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *sea* or *es* and type the whole sentence: *Aunque ___ caro, lo compro.* (Even if it's expensive, I'll buy it.)
yourTurn.why: You don't know the price or you don't care, so *ser* flips to *sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: Even if Altamira offers me more, I'm not selling.
yourTurn.answer: Aunque Altamira me ofrezca más, no vendo.
accept: No vendo aunque Altamira me ofrezca más.
Aunque Altamira me ofrezca más, no voy a vender.
yourTurn.why: *Ofrecer* is an *-er* verb, so the flip to *-a* gives *ofrezca*, and the main verb stays normal.

yourTurn.prompt: Say, to a friend: Even if you're right, I'm not going to sign.
yourTurn.answer: Aunque tengas razón, no voy a firmar.
accept: No voy a firmar aunque tengas razón.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: However much Altamira insists, I'm not going to sign.
yourTurn.answer: Por más que Altamira insista, no voy a firmar.
accept: Por mucho que Altamira insista, no voy a firmar.
yourTurn.why: *Por más que* works like *aunque*: *insistir* is an *-ir* verb, so it takes *-a*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change to a possibility: *Aunque Hernando dice que no, yo voy.* (Even if Hernando says no, I'm going.)
yourTurn.answer: Aunque Hernando diga que no, yo voy.
accept: Yo voy aunque Hernando diga que no.

yourTurn.prompt: Say, to a male friend: Even if you're tired, you have to come.
yourTurn.answer: Aunque estés cansado, tienes que venir.
accept: Aunque estés cansado, tienes que venir.
Tienes que venir aunque estés cansado.
yourTurn.why: *Estar* keeps its accent in the subjunctive: *estés*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. Tomorrow's rain is not a fact yet, and the plain verb states a fact, so Spanish switches to *llueva*.
Almost. English needs even if, but Spanish is just *aunque* plus the subjunctive, with no *si*.
One connector is enough: *aunque* already carries the but.

pitfalls.wrong: Aunque tenga razón, no voy a firmar.
pitfalls.right: Aunque tengas razón, no voy a firmar.
pitfalls.why: Almost. The ending must match who you're talking to: *tengas* for you, *tenga* for him or her.

personal: What would you do even if it were hard or got expensive? Write two true sentences that start with *Aunque* plus a subjunctive, like *Aunque sea difícil, voy a seguir.*
